sDescription: Kendrick Lamar secured the No. 1 spot on the UK chart with his sixth studio album, GNX, marking his second chart-topper in the region following 2015's To Pimp a Butterfly. On the global Spotify chart, GNX pulled in more than 44.2 million streams on its first day, averaging over 3.6 million per track even though it was released only seven hours beforehand. Domestically, the album entered the Billboard 200 at No. 1 with 319,000 album-equivalent units, backed by 379.72 million official on-demand streams.

American musician and songwriter Irving Burgie, considered among the greatest composers of Caribbean music, passed away at the age of 95. He wrote 34 tracks for Harry Belafonte, which included eight out of the 11 tracks featured on the 1956 Belafonte album Calypso, marking the initial record of any sort to reach one million in sales. In 2007, he became an inductee of the Songwriters Hall of Fame.

Dick Dodd, who served as the drummer and singer for The Standells on their 1966 hit song 'Dirty Water', passed away from cancer at age 68. The track grew into an anthem for sports fans in Boston because of its refrain "Boston, you're my home," even though the band possessed no direct ties to the city.

Susan Boyle achieved a No.1 position on the UK chart with her album, marking the best-selling debut in UK chart history. The 48 year-old runner-up in ITV's Britain's Got Talent sold 410,000 copies of 'I Dreamed a Dream'. Additionally, Boyle reached the top of the US charts, establishing a first-week sales record for a female debut album after selling 701,000 copies in its opening week.

Former Lynyrd Skynyrd drummer Artimus Pyle, a convicted sex offender, was arrested for failing to properly register a new permanent address. The 59-year-old had pleaded guilty in 1993 to charges of attempted capital sexual battery by an adult on a victim younger than 12 and being principal to lewd and lascivious behavior on a child younger than 16. He was sentenced to eight years of probation.

Morrissey prepared to take legal action against the UK music weekly the NME when it did not issue an apology regarding an article about his immigration perspectives. The publication targeted the 48-year-old vocalist and ex-Smiths member because he purportedly stated to a journalist that the UK had surrendered its identity owing to high immigration rates.

Control, a biopic following the late Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis, won five awards at the British Independent Film Awards. Produced on a budget of only £3m, the black-and-white movie featured music by New Order, The Killers and David Bowie on its soundtrack.

Pop Idol creator Simon Fuller resolved his £100m copyright lawsuit out of court with Simon Cowell from the X Factor, securing a partnership in the X Factor program. Brought before London's High Court, Mr Fuller's action alleged that the ITV talent show X Factor, created by Mr Cowell, plagiarized his Pop Idol format. The resolution included Mr Cowell's commitment to participate in a minimum of five additional seasons of American Idol.

At the Secrets Postcard Sale hosted at London's Royal College of Art, three canvases created by Sir Paul McCartney were purchased for the price of £35 apiece. Because the identity of each artist was revealed exclusively following the purchase, buyers took a gamble on acquiring celebrity artwork at a greatly reduced price.

Beatles guitarist George Harrison died in Los Angeles of lung cancer aged 58. Following the breakup of The Beatles Harrison had a successful career as a solo artist and later as part of the Traveling Wilburys. The youngest member of The Beatles, (aged 16 when he joined), his compositions include ‘Taxman’, ‘Here Comes the Sun’, ‘Something’, and ‘While My Guitar Gently Weeps’. Harrison released the acclaimed triple album, All Things Must Pass, in 1970, from which came the worldwide No.1 single 'My Sweet Lord.'

U2 member Larry Mullen aided a motorcyclist following a crash. While driving home, Larry noticed the wrecked motorcycle, used his phone to call for assistance, and stayed at the scene until the ambulance showed up.

Johnnie Johnson, who played piano for Chuck Berry over a long period, filed a lawsuit against the rock figure claiming he composed the music for 52 classic songs by Berry. A judge dismissed the case because the statute of limitations for the claims had expired.

Curtis Knight, an American singer and bandleader, passed away at the age of 54. During the 1960s, Jimi Hendrix played in his band. Despite his brief time in the group, Hendrix appeared on more than 60 tracks—comprising 26 studio and 35 live recordings—certain of which have been issued on record.

A collaborative version of "Perfect Day" featuring 29 major artists, among them Elton John, Bono, Tom Jones, and David Bowie, claimed the No. 1 spot on the UK singles chart as a fundraising single for the BBC Children In Need charity. The track was initially composed and recorded in 1973 by Lou Reed.

Whitney Houston withdrew from a Moonie-sponsored concert two hours prior to her scheduled performance upon discovering that the gathering involved a mass wedding for more than 1,000 Moonie couples. The religious organization stated they would not pursue a lawsuit on the condition that the singer gave back the $1m payment she had been given.

Bon Jovi achieved their initial major hit in the US when "You Give Love A Bad Name" claimed the No.1 spot. The track was co-authored by band leaders Jon Bon Jovi and Richie Sambora alongside Desmond Child, a songwriter recognized for his contributions to "I Was Made For Lovin' You" by Kiss and "Dude (Looks Like A Lady)" by Aerosmith. The subsequent single by Bon Jovi, "Livin' On A Prayer," was crafted by this same three-person songwriting team.

sArtist: Now That's What I Call Music
sBand: Now That's What I Call Music
sDescription: Originally launched in the UK to anthologise contemporary chart hits, the Now That's What I Call Music series derived its name from a 1930s Danish bacon advertising poster depicting a pig listening to a singing chicken and saying, "Now, That's What I Call Music." The initial volume featured You Can't Hurry Love by Phil Collins as its opening track, alongside popular songs such as 'Karma Chameleon', 'Red Red Wine', and 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart'. Volume 44 from 1999 stands as the most successful installment and the largest-selling compilation album in history, moving 2.3 million copies and beginning with Britney Spears' ...Baby One More Time.

The album Double Fantasy by John and Yoko was released in 1980. Despite initial poor reception, the album became notable for its association with Lennon's murder three weeks after its release. Following this event, the record achieved worldwide commercial success and subsequently won Album of the Year at the 24th Annual Grammy Awards in 1981.

ABBA achieved their final and ninth No.1 single in the UK with "Super Trouper", marking the band's 25th Top 40 hit in the country. The title "Super Trouper" came from the large spotlights utilized during stadium performances.

A concert by the Sex Pistols scheduled at Lancaster Poly in England was called off by the local council. A statement released by the council explained the decision, stating: 'We don't want that sort of filth (The Sex Pistols) in the town limits.'

At the Broken Arrow Ranch located in Woodside, California, Neil Young tracked the song 'Like a Hurricane'. Several years afterward, the track came out on the album American Stars 'n Bars. Throughout the rest of Young's career, the track has stayed a concert staple and a favorite among fans.

The Beatles achieved their twenty-sixth US single release and eighteenth US No.1 with 'Come Together / Something', which reached the top of the US singles chart. Lennon drew inspiration for the track from Timothy Leary's gubernatorial campaign against Ronald Reagan in California, which used the slogan "Come together, join the party". ’Something’ marked the initial instance where a composition by George Harrison served as an A-side for the group.
During a North American tour, The Stones performed at The Denver Coliseum in Colorado, prompting Colorado Governor John A. Love to proclaim a Rolling Stones day across the state.
Before its release in the UK, I Want to Hold Your Hand by The Beatles achieved advanced orders exceeding one million for the first time in the country.

American rapper Jayceon Terrell Taylor, known as The Game, reached No. 1 in the US in 2005 with his debut album, The Documentary. The 2006 follow-up, Doctor's Advocate, achieved double platinum certification and earned two Grammy Award nominations for its single 'Hate It or Love It' (featuring 50 Cent), in the categories of Best Rap Song and Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group. In 2011, entry to Canada was refused to Game due to alleged Los Angeles gang ties, with concert organisers stating he was associated with the Bloods, an African American street gang.

Filipino-American rapper, singer and record producer Apl.De.Ap achieved a US and UK No.1 single in 2003 titled 'Where Is The Love' with the Black Eyed Peas. Later in 2008, he established the Apl Foundation International (Aplfi) to support children and various communities across the Philippines and Asia.

American musician Keith Carlock has provided drum performances for Toto, Steely Dan, James Taylor, John Mayer, and Sting. During the 2009 Modern Drummer Readers Poll, he received the title of best Pop, Fusion, and All-Around drummer.

Martin Carr, guitarist, singer with English alternative rock band The Boo Radleys, who had the 1995 UK No.9 single 'Wake Up Boo'. Their name is taken from the character Boo Radley in Harper Lee's 1960 novel, To Kill a Mockingbird. After the breakup of the Boo Radleys, Carr launched a solo career, taking the name bravecaptain from a song by the US rock band Firehose.

Jonathan Knight is a member of the American boy band New Kids on the Block. The group scored a UK No.1 single in 1989 with 'You Got It, The Right Stuff' and a US No.1 single in 1990 with 'Step By Step'. Achieving success throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s, they have worldwide record sales exceeding 80 million.

Wendy Wu belonged to the English new wave band the Photos, which achieved a top 5 album on the UK Albums Chart in 1980. Afterward, Wu put out a few solo singles across 1982 and 1983, before partnering with Steve Strange in 1986 to create the duo Strange Cruise.

Michael Dempsey is the bassist for the English new wave group The Lotus Eaters, known for their 1983 UK No. 15 single 'First Picture Of You', which also charted successfully across continental Europe, particularly in France, Italy, Belgium, and Spain. Additionally, Dempsey has collaborated with The Cure and Associates.

Jennifer Batten is an American guitarist whose career includes work as a solo artist and session musician. She performed during all three world tours undertaken by Michael Jackson, and she subsequently spent the years 1999 to 2001 recording and touring alongside Jeff Beck.

Chris Bailey was an Australian singer, songwriter, musician, and producer, as well as the co-founder and vocalist of the rock group the Saints. Their 1976 debut single, '(I'm) Stranded', has been described as "one of the iconic singles of the era" and came out before the first releases from contemporary punk groups like the Sex Pistols, Buzzcocks, and The Clash. Australian Musician magazine named it the fourth most important moment in Australian pop and rock history in 2007. Bailey passed away on 9 April 2022 at the age of 65.

Barry Goudreau played guitar for Boston, whose work includes the 1977 UK No.22 single 'More Than A Feeling' and the 1986 US No.1 single 'Amanda'. As one of the world's best-selling artists, Boston have achieved worldwide sales of more than 75 million records, which includes 31 million albums in the United States. Within the US total, their self-titled debut album accounted for 17 million copies and their second album, Don't Look Back, accounted for seven million.

Roger Troutman was an American composer, songwriter, producer, multi-instrumentalist and the founder of the band Zapp who helped spearhead the funk movement and heavily influenced west coast hip hop due to the scene's heavy sampling of his music over the years. Troutman was found shot and critically wounded outside his northwest Dayton recording studio on 25th April 1999.

American musician and guitarist Ronnie Montrose played in the band Montrose, whose 1973 debut album has often been cited as "America's answer to Led Zeppelin", and the Edgar Winter Group, which released the 1973 single 'Frankenstein' that reached No. 1 in the US and No. 18 in the UK. Alongside his work as a session musician with numerous other artists, he died at the age of 64 on 3 March 2012 from a self-inflicted gunshot wound after taking his own life.

Felix Cavaliere played keyboards for the American rock band The Rascals, which was initially known as The Young Rascals. The group achieved US No.1 hits with the songs 'Good Lovin'' in 1966, 'Groovin'' in 1967, and 'People Got to Be Free' in 1968.

Twink (John Alder) is an English drummer, singer, songwriter, and a key figure in the English psychedelic movement who played in The Pretty Things and The Pink Fairies. In 1967, Twink recorded as part of Santa Barbara Machine Head alongside Ronnie Wood, Kim Gardner, who later joined Ashton, Gardner & Dyke, and keyboardist Jon Lord, who subsequently joined Deep Purple. Later on, Twink converted to Islam and took the name Mohammed Abdullah.

Tim Davis was an American drummer, singer, songwriter, and co-founder of the Steve Miller Band. The band achieved the 1974 US No.1 and 1990 UK No.1 single 'The Joker', the 1976 hit 'Fly Like an Eagle', and the 1982 US No.1 hit 'Abracadabra'. He passed away on September 20, 1988, at the age of 44.

American singer Jody Miller achieved commercial success across the country, folk, and pop genres. Her 1965 song 'Queen of the House', created as an answer song to Roger Miller's 'King of the Road', led to her becoming the second female artist to win a country music accolade from the Grammy Awards. Miller passed away on October 6, 2022, at the age of 80.

Denny Doherty was a member of the American folk rock vocal group The Mamas & the Papas, known for the 1965 hit 'California Dreamin'', the 1966 US No.1 single 'Monday Monday', and the 1967 hit 'Dedicated to the One I Love'. Following a short illness, Doherty passed away on 19th Jan 2007 at the age of 66. His musical career began in 1956 as part of a band named the Hepsters, and he later formed a friendship in 1963 with Cass Elliot during her time with The Big 3.

American flugelhorn player, trumpeter and composer Chuck Mangione, whose single 'Feels So Good' reached No.4 in the US in 1978, passed away in his sleep at his home in Rochester on July 22, 2025, at the age of 84.

American record producer and musician, Meco Monardo, who had the 1977 US No.1 & UK No.7 single 'Star Wars Theme'. As a session musician, he played the trombone with acts like Diana Ross. He performed on Diana Ross' 1980 album Diana as a favour to producer (and neighbour) Nile Rodgers. His solo on the single 'I'm Coming Out' is notable because of the rarity of trombone features on post-big-band era pop records.

John Mayall was an English blues and rock musician, songwriter, and producer, known as the 'father of the UK blues movement'. His Bluesbreakers Band featured Eric Clapton, Mick Taylor, Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Jack Bruce, Peter Green, and Jimmy McCulloch. His career spanned nearly seven decades, and he remained an active musician until his death. Mayall passed away at his California home on 22 July 2024 at the age of 90.

Country singer and songwriter Merle Travis gained renown for his distinct guitar playing, a technique still called Travis picking within the guitar community. Among his songwriting credits is 'Sixteen Tons', which became a US No.1 hit for Ernie Ford in 1955. His career honors include an induction into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970 and election to the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1977. Travis passed away from a heart attack at his residence in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, on 20th October 1983.
